summary:
Guam stands under the United States federal framework as an unincorporated territory, and its own local law adds specific protections and specific conditions for trans visitors.

Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression is prohibited locally. In August 2015 the Guam Legislature passed Bill 102-33 unanimously, banning discrimination in private employment on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, and separately forbidding discrimination against government employees on grounds of sexuality or identity.

Legal gender recognition requires surgery. To amend a birth certificate, a trans person must give the Office of Vital Statistics a sworn statement from a physician confirming sex reassignment surgery. The Motor Vehicle Division issues an amended driver's licence on receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed. A 2018 bill that would have permitted legal gender change on judicial permission with a supporting letter from a licensed professional and no surgery requirement failed on 17 December 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote after the Legislature postponed action on 13 December 2018, so surgery remains the condition.

On partner recognition, chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015 following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero, who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making Guam the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

A January 2025 executive order banning transgender troops from serving openly applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent United States military presence; the order directs the Secretary of Defense to submit an implementation plan within 30 days and frames trans identity as "radical gender ideology."
tangentialFactors:
Federal law has covered hate crimes motivated by gender identity since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act.

Guam is regarded as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people, with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment; this is a general LGBTQ finding rather than a transgender-specific one. The Chamorro people have traditionally accepted homosexuality and transgender people, and homosexuality was never viewed as taboo in Chamorro society.

A visible LGBTQ social scene has existed since the 1990s, with a handful of nightclubs and social functions and annual Guam Pride held since 2017 attracting a few hundred people. Guam is a member of the International Gay and Lesbian Travel Association and has begun commercialising itself as a tourist destination for LGBTQ people; these are general LGBTQ observations, not trans-specific findings.
localsOnly:
Local employment protections under Bill 102-33 cover Guam residents in private employment and separately bar discrimination against government employees on grounds of sexuality or identity.

Legal gender recognition for residents requires surgery: the Office of Vital Statistics amends a birth certificate only on a sworn physician statement confirming sex reassignment surgery, and the Motor Vehicle Division issues an amended driver's licence on the same condition. The 2018 reform bill (introduced in May 2018 by Senator Fernando Esteves) would have allowed legal gender change on judicial permission with a supporting letter from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional and no surgery requirement, but the Legislature postponed a vote on 13 December 2018 pending medical and law-enforcement process issues and the bill failed on 17 December 2018 by 6 to 7.

Private adult consensual and non-commercial homosexual acts have been legal in Guam since the Criminal Code reform of 1978. The 1933 penal code ordained by the Naval Governor, identical to California's, prohibited sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus whether heterosexual or homosexual with one to ten years' imprisonment. The only reported sodomy case in Guam occurred in the early 1950s in Pennington v Government, which the defendant won solely on procedural grounds when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held the trial court had been without authority to try Pennington without a jury.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not document any trans-specific violence incidents, enforcement actions under Bill 102-33, or hate-crime prosecutions in Guam motivated by gender identity; the absence of such reports is not sourced as evidence that none occur.

Whether Guam's local employment non-discrimination protections have been tested in practice, and how the surgery requirement for legal gender recognition is applied at present, are unresolved on the available sources.
